# Introduction

Today you will practice more R skills. You will start from an empty
Quarto file and build it up with a header, text, code chunks, and data,
working with vectors, data frames, if/else, and for loops along the
way.

## Learning goals

In this lab, you will...

- create a Quarto document from an empty file, with a header, headings,
  text, and code chunks;
- make vectors, pick out values by position and by condition, and
  count with `TRUE`/`FALSE`;
- build a data frame from vectors, load one from a CSV file, and add a
  column;
- make a decision with `if`/`else` for one value, `ifelse()` for a
  whole column, and `case_when()` for more than two groups;
- repeat a step with a `for` loop and store the results;
- see how an AI agent works on files, and why you check its work
  yourself.

## Get ready

Find your repo beginning with `lab-08` in the
[statistical-history organization](https://github.com/statistical-history)
and clone it in RStudio using **File → New Project → Version Control →
Git** and its SSH address. The repo contains only a `data/` folder and
a `messy-project/` folder. There is no document yet, because you are
about to make it.

# Part 1 — Start from an empty file

1. **Create the file.** Choose **File → New File → Quarto Document…**,
   then click **Create Empty Document** in the bottom-left corner of the
   dialog.
2. **Switch to Source view.** At the top left of the editor, click
   **Source** (not **Visual**), so that you see exactly what you type.
3. **Save it.** Choose **File → Save** and name it `lab-08.qmd`. Save it
   in the **top folder of your repo**, the same folder that contains
   `data/`. Where you save it matters: your code will look for data
   relative to this file.
4. **Add a header.** The YAML header goes at the very top, between two
   lines of three dashes. It holds the document's settings:

    ```yaml
    ---
    title: "Lab 08"
    author: "Your name"
    format: pdf
    ---
    ```

5. **Render.** Click **Render**. You get a PDF with a title and nothing
   else. That is your first working document.
6. **Add a heading and a sentence.** Below the header, leave a blank
   line, then type a level-1 heading such as `# Vectors`. Under it,
   write a sentence in plain text. In Markdown, `#` makes a heading,
   `**bold**` makes **bold**, and `*italic*` makes *italic*.
7. **Add a code chunk.** Use the **+C** button at the top of the editor,
   **Code → Insert Chunk**, or the keyboard shortcut **Cmd + Option + I**
   (Mac) or **Ctrl + Alt + I** (Windows). If the shortcut opens your
   browser's developer tools instead, close them and use **+C**. A chunk starts with ```` ```{r} ```` and
   ends with ```` ``` ````. Everything between those lines is R code.
   Run a chunk with its green ▶ button, and render to see the code and
   its output in the PDF.

From now on, use one level-1 heading (`#`) for each part of the lab.
Put each **Your turn** answer under its part, with the question number
in bold (for example, `**2.1**`). Code goes in chunks, and written
answers go in plain text below them.

**1.1** Put your name in the `author:` line. Add the heading `# Part 2:
Vectors`, a sentence of your own, and an empty chunk below it. Render,
and check that the PDF shows all three.

# Part 2 — Vectors

A **vector** is an ordered set of values of the same type: all
numbers, all text (*character*), or all `TRUE`/`FALSE` (*logical*).

Type each chunk below into your document under `# Part 2: Vectors`.
Run it with the green ▶ button, and check that your output matches the
output shown here.

**Make a vector.** `c()` combines values into one vector. `length()`
counts the values, and `class()` tells you their type.

```{r}
#| label: demo-vectors
scores <- c(88, 92, 75, 64, 99)
scores
length(scores)
mean(scores)
class(scores)
```

**Pick values by position.** Square brackets pick values out of a
vector. Positions start at 1, so `scores[2]` is the second score, and
`scores[c(1, 3)]` gives the first and third.

```{r}
#| label: demo-positions
scores[2]
scores[c(1, 3)]
```

**Pick values by a condition.** `scores > 80` asks "is this score above
80?" once for each value, so you get one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per score.
Put that condition inside the square brackets to keep only the values
where it is `TRUE`. `sum()` counts the `TRUE`s, because R treats `TRUE`
as 1 and `FALSE` as 0. The other comparisons work the same way: `<`,
`>=`, `<=`, `==` (equal), and `!=` (not equal).

```{r}
#| label: demo-conditions
scores > 80
scores[scores > 80]
sum(scores > 80)
```

**Use one vector to pick from another.** The names in `students` line
up with `scores` position by position, so a condition on `scores` picks
out the matching names. Part 3 builds on this idea: a data frame is
vectors lined up side by side.

```{r}
#| label: demo-two-vectors
students <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli")
class(students)
students[scores > 80]
```

**One type per vector.** If you mix types, R turns every value into
text. Notice the quotes in the output:

```{r}
#| label: demo-one-type
c(1, "a", TRUE)
```

| Day | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| High (°F) | 61 | 58 | 66 | 71 | 69 | 55 | 63 |

**2.1** Save the days as `days` and the temperatures as `temps`. What
is the mean high, and what type (`class()`) is each vector?

**2.2** Which days were warmer than 65°F, and how many were there? Use a
condition inside square brackets, and `sum()`.

# Part 3 — Data frames

A **data frame** is a table whose columns are vectors of the same
length. Each row is one observation. Add the heading
`# Part 3: Data frames`, and type these chunks below it.

**Build a data frame from vectors.** `data.frame()` puts `students` and
`scores` side by side and gives each column a name. `$` pulls one
column back out. A column is just a vector, so everything from Part 2
works on it.

```{r}
#| label: demo-data-frame
class_scores <- data.frame(student = students, score = scores)
class_scores
class_scores$score
mean(class_scores$score)
```

**Choose rows and columns.** Square brackets on a data frame take two
parts, `[rows, columns]`. Leaving a part empty means "all," so
`class_scores[2, ]` is row 2 with every column. A condition in the rows
part keeps the rows where it is `TRUE`.

```{r}
#| label: demo-rows
class_scores[2, ]
class_scores[class_scores$score > 80, ]
```

**Add a column.** Assign to a new column name with `$` and `<-`.

```{r}
#| label: demo-add-column
class_scores$passed <- class_scores$score >= 70
class_scores
```

**Load data.** The file `data/penguins.csv` records 344 penguins from
three islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, measured by Dr. Kristen
Gorman between 2007 and 2009. `read.csv()` reads it into a data frame.
Then `head()` shows the first six rows, `nrow()` counts the rows, and
`names()` lists the columns. Put this in its own chunk.

The path `"data/penguins.csv"` is **relative**: it means "the `data`
folder next to this document." That is why you saved `lab-08.qmd`
beside `data/`. If R says it `cannot open file`, check where your
document is saved.

```{r}
#| label: demo-load-data
penguins <- read.csv("data/penguins.csv")
head(penguins)
nrow(penguins)
names(penguins)
```

**Missing values.** Two penguins have no recorded body mass, and R
stores each missing value as `NA`. `summary()` counts them. A single
`NA` makes the whole mean `NA`, because a mean that includes an unknown
value is unknown. `na.rm = TRUE` leaves the missing values out. That is
a choice, so say so when you report a result.

```{r}
#| label: demo-na
summary(penguins$body_mass_g)
mean(penguins$body_mass_g)
mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
```

**Inline code.** Inline code puts a number from R into a sentence, so
you never type the number yourself. Below the chunk, in plain text (not
inside a chunk), type:

The data contain `` `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(penguins)")` `` penguins.

When you render, R runs the code and the PDF reads: "The data contain
`r nrow(penguins)` penguins." Inline code only works **after** the
chunk that loads the data.

# Part 4 — If and else

`if` lets your code make a decision. If a condition is `TRUE`, R runs
one block of code. Otherwise, it runs the `else` block. Add the heading
`# Part 4: If and else`, and type these chunks below it.

**Decide for one value.** The condition in parentheses must be a single
`TRUE` or `FALSE`. If it is `TRUE`, R runs the code in the first pair of
braces `{ }`. Otherwise, it runs the code after `else`. `print()` shows the result
(you will need it inside loops in Part 5). Run the chunk, then change
`score` to 65 and run it again.

```{r}
#| label: demo-if
score <- 75
if (score >= 70) {
  print("pass")
} else {
  print("fail")
}
```

**More than two cases.** `else if` adds another case. R checks the
conditions in order and stops at the first `TRUE`. That is why this
chain checks 90 before 80: a score of 95 is also at least 80.

```{r}
#| label: demo-else-if
if (score >= 90) {
  print("A")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("B")
} else if (score >= 70) {
  print("C")
} else {
  print("below C")
}
```

**The error you get with a whole vector.** `scores` has five values, so
`scores >= 70` gives five `TRUE`/`FALSE` answers, but `if` needs exactly
one. R stops with the error "the condition has length > 1." An error
normally stops the render too. To show an error in the PDF on purpose,
make `#| error: true` the first line of the chunk, as below. Use it only
when the error is the point.

```{r}
#| label: demo-if-error
#| echo: fenced
#| error: true
if (scores >= 70) print("pass") else print("fail")
```

**Decide for every value.** `ifelse(condition, value if TRUE, value if
FALSE)` makes the same decision for every value of a vector and gives
one answer per value. That makes it the tool for creating a new column.

```{r}
#| label: demo-ifelse
ifelse(scores >= 70, "pass", "fail")
class_scores$result <- ifelse(class_scores$score >= 70, "pass", "fail")
class_scores
```

The same idea works on the penguins. A penguin with no recorded mass
gets `NA` as its size: `NA` in, `NA` out. Compare the two tables below.
By default, `table()` quietly leaves out the `NA`s, so its counts add
up to 342, not 344. `useNA = "ifany"` adds a column for the missing
values whenever there are any.

```{r}
#| label: demo-ifelse-penguins
penguins$size <- ifelse(penguins$body_mass_g > 4000, "large", "small")
table(penguins$size)
table(penguins$size, useNA = "ifany")
```

**More than two groups for every value.** `ifelse()` splits values two
ways. For more groups, use `case_when()` from the dplyr package, which
loads with the tidyverse, as in Labs 06 and 07. Loading it prints a
list of packages and "conflicts"; that is normal. Each line is
`condition ~ value`; read `~` as "then." Like an `else if` chain,
`case_when()` checks the conditions in order and uses the first one
that is `TRUE`, so a 6000 g penguin is "very large," not "large."

**With a catch-all.** `.default = "small"` means "everything else is
small," like a final `else`. (Older code writes the same thing as
`TRUE ~ "small"`.)

```{r}
#| label: demo-case-when-default
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
penguins$size_catchall <- case_when(
  penguins$body_mass_g >= 5500 ~ "very large",
  penguins$body_mass_g >= 4500 ~ "large",
  penguins$body_mass_g >= 3500 ~ "medium",
  .default = "small"
)
table(penguins$size_catchall, useNA = "ifany")
```

Look at the table: 73 small penguins and no `NA`. The catch-all also
caught the two penguins with no recorded mass and called them small.

**Without a catch-all.** Name the last group with its own condition
instead. A penguin that matches no condition gets `NA`, so the two
penguins with no mass stay missing, and the small count drops to 71.

```{r}
#| label: demo-case-when
penguins$size_group <- case_when(
  penguins$body_mass_g >= 5500 ~ "very large",
  penguins$body_mass_g >= 4500 ~ "large",
  penguins$body_mass_g >= 3500 ~ "medium",
  penguins$body_mass_g < 3500 ~ "small"
)
table(penguins$size_group, useNA = "ifany")
```

Use a catch-all only when you are sure every value that reaches it
belongs in that group.

# Part 5 — For loops

A **for loop** repeats a block of code once for each value of a
vector. Add the heading `# Part 5: For loops`, and type these chunks
below it.

**Loop over numbers.** Read `for (i in 1:3)` as "for each `i` in 1, 2,
3, run the code in the braces." Each time through the loop, `i` takes
the next value. Inside a loop, R does **not** show values
automatically, so use `print()`.

```{r}
#| label: demo-for
for (i in 1:3) {
  print(i)
}
```

**Loop over text.** You can loop over any vector, including text.
`paste()` joins pieces of text with a space between them.

```{r}
#| label: demo-for-text
for (s in students) {
  print(paste("Hello,", s))
}
```

**Store the results.** To keep what a loop computes, make an empty
vector **before** the loop. `numeric(5)` is five zeros. Each time
through the loop, fill position `i`.

```{r}
#| label: demo-for-store
squares <- numeric(5)
for (i in 1:5) {
  squares[i] <- i^2
}
squares
```

**Put an `if` inside a loop.** The loop visits each student, and the
`if` decides whether to print anything for that student.

```{r}
#| label: demo-for-if
for (i in 1:5) {
  if (scores[i] >= 90) {
    print(paste(students[i], "got an A"))
  }
}
```

**Put it all together.** This loop finds the mean body mass of each
penguin species. Each time through, `rows` is a `TRUE`/`FALSE` vector
that marks the penguins of one species. The mean of their masses, with
`na.rm = TRUE`, goes into position `i` of `mean_mass`. R has shortcuts
that do this in one line, such as `tapply()`, but the loop shows the
steps.

```{r}
#| label: demo-for-species
species <- c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo")
mean_mass <- numeric(3)
for (i in 1:3) {
  rows <- penguins$species == species[i]
  mean_mass[i] <- mean(penguins$body_mass_g[rows], na.rm = TRUE)
}
data.frame(species = species, mean_mass = round(mean_mass))
```

## Chat versus agent

So far you have used AI in a **chat**: you ask, it answers, and you
decide what to do. **Codex** is an **agent**. You point it at a folder,
and it reads the files there, runs commands, and creates, moves, and
edits files itself.

| | Chat (ChatGPT, DukeGPT) | Agent (Codex) |
|---|---|---|
| What it sees | What you paste in | Every file in the folder you open |
| What it does | Writes an answer | Runs commands and changes files |
| What you check | The answer | The answer **and** every change it made |

The course AI policy applies, and it matters more when the tool acts.
From the [syllabus](https://statistical-history.github.io/syllabus.html):
**first make a genuine attempt yourself**; **verify the output and
revise anything you use**; and **you must be able to explain every line
of code that you submit.** For any work materially informed by AI,
record the tool and model, the date, and a link to the complete
transcript.

Duke OIT's [Codex best
practices](https://codex-best-practices-d67bea.pages.oit.duke.edu/best-practices/security.html)
add four habits. Follow them whenever you use Codex:

| Habit | Why |
|---|---|
| Open the **narrowest folder** that holds the work, never your home folder or Desktop | Codex can only change what it can see |
| Choose **Work in: This computer** and the permission mode **Ask for approval** | Codex has to ask before it goes beyond that folder or uses the internet |
| Read every command before approving it | You are responsible for what runs |
| Never put passwords, keys, or identifying participant data in the folder or the prompt | The agent may read anything in the folder |

## The messy project

`messy-project/` belongs to a pretend group. They timed coffee lines at
three spots on campus, and their notes say the median waits were
**library cafe 5 min, union cart 3 min, gym smoothie bar 7 min**. The
data are invented. You can open every file in it from RStudio's
**Files** pane.

**6.1** *(Before Codex sees the folder: your genuine attempt.)* Look through
`messy-project/` with your group. In your document, under `# Part 6:
AI agent`, list the problems that would stop someone else from
reproducing the three medians. Which clean file is the current one?
Which script runs first? What would break on another computer?

## The prompts

Send these four prompts one at a time, in order. Read each answer
before you send the next one, and compare it with your list from 6.1.
When Codex asks to run a command, read the command and make sure you
know what it does before you approve it.

**Prompt 1: look and plan, without changing anything.**

> This folder is a small R project. A group timed waits at three coffee
> spots, and `notes.txt` gives their results: median wait 5 minutes at
> the library cafe, 3 at the union cart, and 7 at the gym smoothie bar.
> Don't change any files yet. Read every file and tell me (1) which
> files actually produce those results, (2) the order the scripts have
> to run in, and (3) anything that would stop a classmate from
> reproducing the results on a different computer. Then propose a
> clearer folder structure.

**Prompt 2: reorganize, with rules.**

> Go ahead with the reorganization, following these rules. Don't delete
> anything: move files that are no longer used into an `archive/`
> folder. Keep the raw data separate from the cleaned data. Remove the
> `setwd()` line and make every file path relative to this project
> folder. Update the paths inside the scripts so they still work after
> the move. Don't change any calculations.

**Prompt 3: write the README.**

> Write a `README.md` for this folder that lets a classmate reproduce
> the three median wait times from scratch in RStudio. Include a
> one-paragraph description of the project; numbered steps in the order
> to run them, including how to set the working directory; a short
> description of each file; the data-cleaning decisions from
> `notes.txt`; and the expected results, so the reader can check them.

**Prompt 4: report and check.**

> List every file you moved, created, or edited, and what you changed
> in each one. Did you run the R code to confirm the medians are still
> 5, 3, and 7? If you didn't, say so.

## Check the README by following it

An AI agent's README is a claim. Test it the only way that counts:
follow it **exactly as written** on a computer that has never seen the
folder.

1. On your laptop, compress the reorganized `messy-project` folder into
   a zip file.
2. In RStudio's **Files** pane, click **Home** so that you are outside
   your `lab-08` repo. Then use **Upload** to upload the zip. RStudio
   unzips it.
3. Follow the README step by step, doing exactly what it says and
   nothing more.

Do you get 5, 3, and 7? Where was the README wrong, unclear, or missing
a step? In class, Kat does this on the projector while one of you reads
the steps out loud.

## Taking this to your project

Milestone 3 asks that "a reader can follow what happened and reproduce
the main numbers." If you use Codex on your group's project repository:

- Work in your own clone of the repo, and **commit and push first**.
  Then git shows every change Codex makes, and you can undo any of
  them.
- Open only the project folder, and use **Ask for approval**.
- Keep participant data non-identifying, as the project instructions
  already require.
- Test the README the way we did today: have someone who did not write
  it follow it from a fresh copy.
- Follow the syllabus. Record the tool, model, date, and transcript.
- If Codex or another AI agent helped write your README, **disclose
  that in the README itself**: name the agent and say what it did.

# Syntax you saw today

| Task | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Make a vector | `x <- c(4, 8, 15)`; `1:7` |
| Values by position | `x[2]`; `x[c(1, 3)]` |
| Values by condition | `x[x > 5]` |
| Count `TRUE`s | `sum(x > 5)` |
| Data frame from vectors | `dat <- data.frame(a = x, b = y)` |
| One column; add a column | `dat$a`; `dat$new <- dat$a * 2` |
| Rows and columns | `dat[dat$a > 5, ]`; `dat[ , "b"]` |
| Read a CSV | `dat <- read.csv("data/file.csv")` |
| Ignore missing values | `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` |
| Decide for one value | `if (condition) { ... } else { ... }` |
| Decide for every value | `ifelse(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)` |
| Decide among several groups | `case_when(condition1 ~ value1, condition2 ~ value2)` |
| Repeat | `for (i in 1:n) { ... }` |
| Store loop results | `out <- numeric(n)`, then `out[i] <- ...` inside the loop |
| Inline code | `` `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(dat)")` `` |
| Show an error without stopping the render | `#| error: true` at the top of the chunk |

  (objects, vectors, data frames), chapter 9 ("Programs": `if` and
  `else`), and chapter 11 ("Loops").
- Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund, [*R for
  Data Science* (2e)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/), chapter 2 ("Workflow:
  basics") and chapter 28 ("Quarto").
- Quarto, [Tutorial: Hello,
  Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/hello/rstudio.html) and
  [Markdown
  Basics](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html).
- Allison Horst, Alison Hill, and Kristen Gorman,
  [palmerpenguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/), for
  the penguin data.
- Duke OIT, [Codex Starter Best
  Practices](https://codex-best-practices-d67bea.pages.oit.duke.edu/best-practices/overview.html),
  for the safety settings in Part 6.
